What the academy teaches

Software architecture is the set of decisions that are hard to change later. The academy teaches how to find them, make them well, describe them and keep them healthy.

Architecture is decisions, not diagrams

The valuable part is which choices were made, why, and what they cost. Pictures are one way to share them.

Quality needs numbers

A goal such as “fast” or “secure” cannot be designed for or tested until it is written as a measurable scenario.

Others must be able to read it

A structure that only its author understands is a risk. Views, interfaces and records exist so the next person can act.

Evidence beats opinion

Compare options against the scenarios that matter most, and say what you assumed and what you checked.

Systems keep changing

Governance, migration and dependency choices decide whether a system can still change in five years.

Agents are now part of the work

AI can draft options and code, and agents can run parts of the system. Both need verification, limits and records of who decided.

The six levels

Understand, document, decide, design with agents, govern, lead. Each level ends in an artefact you can inspect, not only a score.

How learning is assessed

Knowledge is necessary, not sufficient

Each open course combines quiz questions with a lab that builds a real artefact. Higher levels will add reviewed design work and an oral defence, because recognising terms is not the same as designing.

Evidence you can inspect

Every lesson ends in a lab section that adds to one record, so what you built is on the page, not only a score.

Checks that tell the truth

Health checks look for completeness, not for a good design. The pages say so, and rubrics in each lesson show what missing, partial and competent work looks like.

Practice that is separate from assessment

Mock exams are practice. A learner can take a paper again; the readiness report says what is weak. They do not predict an external result.

Separated decisions

When a credential scheme exists, the people who teach a level will not decide whether a candidate meets its standard, and appeals will go to someone who did not assess the candidate.

Design benchmark, not a claim

ISO/IEC 17024:2026 guides how a person-certification scheme should be designed. Intellica makes no accreditation or conformity claim.

What it is built on

Public curricula and standards are used as references and mappings, and every source is dated.

Level 1 follows the topics of the iSAQB Foundation curriculum and Level 2 uses the arc42 template under its licence. See the curriculum mapping and the source register. For the security side of agent systems, see the Cybersecurity for Agentic Environments Academy.

Reviewed 2026-11-25. Intellica is independent of iSAQB, arc42, ISO, IEC, IEEE and the Software Engineering Institute. Mappings show how our lessons relate to published topics. They are not an affiliation, an approval or a prediction of any exam result.
